proof_register.text: A counterexample at any exponent $n\geq3$ would give one at exponent $4$ or at an odd prime exponent.
$x^4+y^4=z^2$ has no solution in positive integers, and therefore Fermat's Last Theorem holds for $n=4$.
Kummer's regular-prime criterion and his theorem for regular prime exponents are stated.
The first case of Fermat's Last Theorem for $n=3$ is ruled out in the Eisenstein integers.
The second case for $n=3$ is outlined, not proved; the unit analysis inside the descent remains compressed.
Unique factorisation is shown to fail by an explicit double factorisation in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$.

$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and $G_{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ as a profinite group, with decomposition groups and Frobenius elements at unramified primes, defined up to conjugacy.
$\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ exists as the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ for $|\cdot|_\ell$, is a field, and contains $\mathbb{Q}$ as a dense subfield.
Essay 01's step that coprime factors of a perfect power are themselves powers is proved once, for every exponent, as a statement about valuations.

On the congruence side: every compatible sequence has exactly one digit expansion and every digit string occurs, proved for $\varprojlim\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\mathbb{Z}$ directly, without appeal to completeness or to the identification of the two constructions.
Free modules over $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ have well-defined rank, and a matrix lies in $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_\ell)$ exactly when its determinant has valuation $0$.
The metric and congruence constructions agree: $\mathbb{Z}_\ell\cong\varprojlim\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\mathbb{Z}$.
On the valuation-ring side: $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ is a ring whose units are the elements of valuation $0$, so it has the single maximal ideal $\ell\mathbb{Z}_\ell$.
The valuation $v_\ell$ is additive on products and ultrametric on sums, with equality when the valuations differ, and $|\cdot|_\ell$ is multiplicative and non-archimedean.
Continuous $\rho:G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\mathrm{GL}_2(K)$; ramified and unramified primes; the conductor of a representation; irreducibility.

proof_register.short: Traces of Frobenius determine a semisimple representation
proof_register.text: A semisimple two-dimensional representation is determined up to isomorphism by the traces of Frobenius at almost all primes. This is what makes "these two representations agree" a checkable claim in essays 18 and 25.
For $y^2+y=x^3-x^2$, direct calculation gives $\Delta=-11$ and a short integral model whose discriminant is $6^{12}(-11)$.
The genus-one characterization and existence of a general Weierstrass model are stated; its point at infinity and discriminant are defined; the discriminant criterion for smoothness is stated.
proof_register.short: A genus-one curve has a Weierstrass model, and $\Delta\neq0$ is smoothness

proof_register.text: Associativity of chord-and-tangent addition, and hence the full abelian-group theorem for $E(\mathbb{Q})$, is stated rather than proved.
proof_register.short: Associativity of the chord-and-tangent group law

proof_register.text: The chord-and-tangent rule, rational closure and the short-Weierstrass addition formulas are derived.
The point $(0,0)$ on $y^2+y=x^3-x^2$ is shown by direct calculation to have order $5$.
Complex uniformization $E(\mathbb{C})\cong\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is stated, not proved.
Bad reduction at $\ell$ holds exactly when $\ell$ divides $\Delta_{\min}$, so there are finitely many bad primes and one valuation computation finds them all.
At an additive prime $f_\ell\geq2$, with equality for $\ell>3$, and the primes $2$ and $3$ permit larger exponents.
At a prime of multiplicative reduction the conductor exponent is $f_\ell=1$. This is the only conductor exponent the Fermat argument uses, because the Frey curve is semistable.
proof_register.short: Conductor exponent $f_\ell=1$ at a multiplicative prime

proof_register.text: The Hasse bound $|a_\ell|\leq2\sqrt{\ell}$.
Every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ has a global minimal model. The FLT chain does not need this in general: essay 23 exhibits the Frey curve's minimal model and must prove that model minimal.
The trichotomy good / multiplicative / additive follows from the tangent directions at the unique singular point of the reduced cubic, and $a_\ell\in\{0,\pm1\}$ at a bad prime names the type.
Given the conductor exponents, $N_E$ is square-free exactly when $E$ is semistable, and a semistable curve has $N_E=\operatorname{rad}(\Delta_{\min})$.
Reduction at a good prime is injective on torsion of order coprime to $\ell$, which is why $5$ divides every point count of the conductor-$11$ curve.
$y^2+y=x^3-x^2$ is semistable of conductor $11$, split multiplicative at $11$ with $a_{11}=1$; $y^2=x^3+1$ is additive at $2$ and $3$, so it is not semistable.

The Frey curve has full rational $2$-torsion: $x(x-a^p)(x+b^p)$ has three rational roots, so $E[2]\subset E(\mathbb{Q})$. This is the extra structure that may sharpen Mazur's threshold from $p>7$ to $p\geq5$.

$E[n]\cong(\mathbb{Z}/n)^2$ in characteristic zero, and the Tate module $T_\ell(E)=\varprojlim E[\ell^n]$ is free of rank $2$ over $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ -- which is why the representations are $2\times2$.
Mazur's isogeny theorem and the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion will be stated with their hypotheses.

$\Gamma_0(N)$ acting on $\mathbb{H}$, its index $\mu$, and the counts $
u_2$, $
u_3$, $
u_\infty$ of elliptic points and cusps -- exactly the inputs essay 13's formula consumes.
Weight-$k$ modularity, holomorphy at the cusps, $q$-expansions, and the space $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ of weight-2 cusp forms -- without which the phrase "a weight-2 newform of level $N$" is undefined.
The dimension formula for $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ will be derived from the index, elliptic-point counts and cusp count.

The valence formula, that the weighted count of zeros and poles of a weight-$k$ form equals $k\mu/12$. Imported: its proof is a contour integral around the fundamental domain and would cost an essay of its own. Essay 13 derives the dimension formula from it.

proof_register.short: A simultaneous Hecke eigenbasis exists for $\gcd(n,N)=1$
proof_register.text: The Hecke operators $T_n$ with $\gcd(n,N)=1$ are simultaneously diagonalisable on $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$. Imported: the Petersson inner product and self-adjointness are a course, and the chain needs only the conclusion.
For a normalised eigenform, $a_1=1$ forces the Hecke eigenvalues to be the Fourier coefficients, and the coefficients are multiplicative -- the step that makes $a_\ell(f)$ mean anything.

proof_register.short: Newform theory, and the level of a newform
proof_register.text: The decomposition of $S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ into old and new subspaces, and the well-definedness of the level of a newform. Imported: Atkin--Lehner theory. Without it "the level" in Ribet's theorem is undefined.
Eichler–Shimura will be stated, not proved.

$L(E,s)$ and $L(f,s)$ as Euler products, and the analytic continuation and functional equation. Motivating rather than load-bearing: modularity is stated representation-theoretically, so the chain never evaluates an $L$-function.
The Modularity Theorem will be stated, not proved.
Wiles's deformation-theoretic machinery will be described as an anatomy, not presented as a proof.
Langlands–Tunnell will be stated, not proved.
A normalised hypothetical Fermat solution produces the Frey curve $y^2=x(x-a^p)(x+b^p)$.
The displayed Frey model has discriminant $16(abc)^{2p}$.

The substitution $x=4X$, $y=8Y+4X$ yields an integral model with $a_1=1$, minimal at $2$, of discriminant $\Delta_{\min}=2^{-8}(abc)^{2p}$, so the FLT chain needs no appeal to the general existence theorem for minimal models.

The Frey curve has multiplicative reduction at every bad prime -- at odd primes because pairwise coprimality forbids a triple root, and at $2$ because $a_1=1$ makes the tangent cone separable -- hence it is semistable with conductor $\operatorname{rad}(abc)$.

proof_register.short: The Modularity Theorem applied to the Frey curve, from essay 18
proof_register.text: Essay 18's Modularity Theorem for semistable curves is applied to $E$, giving a weight-2 newform of level $\operatorname{rad}(abc)$ with the same Galois representation.

What each normalisation buys: $A\equiv-1\pmod4$ and $16\mid B$ give integrality of the minimal model, while the extra factor of $2$ in $32\mid B$ is what makes $2$ a bad prime and puts it in the conductor.
The conductor of the Frey curve's mod $p$ representation will be established, with the irreducibility threshold handled explicitly.

The final contradiction is assembled conditionally on the explicit inputs assigned to essays 13, 18, 23 and 24, and the collection's full FLT conclusion also still owes the outlined second case for $n=3$.
The level-$2$ arithmetic is computed, but its dimension formula remains owed by essay 13.
Ribet's level-lowering theorem is stated with the hypotheses used by the closing argument.

proof_register.short: Fermat's Last Theorem for $n=5$ and $n=7$, classical and external to this collection
proof_register.text: The Frey-curve route needs $\bar\rho$ irreducible, which Mazur's isogeny theorem supplies only outside a finite exceptional set containing $5$ and $7$. The exponents $5$ and $7$ are therefore handled by classical work outside this collection — Dirichlet and Legendre in 1825, Lamé in 1839 — and that dependency is recorded here rather than left implicit.
